tagline: Digital nation of forests and song
overview:
Estonia is the northernmost of the three Baltic states, facing Finland across the Gulf of Finland and Sweden across the Baltic Sea, with Latvia to the south and Russia to the east. It is about the size of New Hampshire and Vermont combined, and half of it is forest. The capital, Tallinn, has one of the best-preserved medieval old towns in Europe, a cluster of towers, guild halls, and cobbled lanes that looks like a storybook, right next to glass office buildings full of software start-ups.

Only about 1.3 million people live in Estonia, and they speak Estonian, a language related to Finnish rather than to the languages of its other neighbors. Estonia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and is a parliamentary republic, a member of the European Union and NATO, and a pioneer of digital government: citizens vote, sign documents, and start companies online, and nearly every school is connected. Estonians are known for quiet reserve, a deep love of nature, and mass choir festivals that gather tens of thousands of singers.
landAndNature: Estonia is flat and low, with its highest point, Suur Munamägi, just 318 meters above sea level. Forests of pine, spruce, and birch cover about half the land, and huge peat bogs, crossed by wooden boardwalks, cover much of the rest; Soomaa National Park floods so deeply each spring that locals call it the fifth season and travel by canoe. More than 2,000 islands lie off the coast, the largest being Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, with windmills, juniper heaths, and a meteorite crater at Kaali. Wolves, lynx, brown bears, and moose live in the forests, and flying squirrels glide between trees in the east. Lake Peipus, shared with Russia, is one of Europe's largest lakes. Winters are long, dark, and snowy, and the sea often freezes.
peopleAndCulture: Estonians treasure singing. Every five years the Song Celebration in Tallinn brings together up to 30,000 singers on one stage before crowds of 100,000, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Traditional foods include black rye bread, which is served with nearly every meal, sour cream, pickled herring, and blood sausage at Christmas, while kama, a roasted grain flour mixed with yogurt, is a favorite snack. Midsummer, called Jaanipäev, is celebrated with bonfires that burn all through the short night. Saunas are part of weekly life, and in winter people cut holes in the ice to swim. Cross-country skiing, basketball, and wrestling are popular, and Estonia is known for inventing the video-calling service Skype and for its love of wife-carrying and kiiking, swinging a full 360 degrees on a giant swing.
history: Finnic tribes have lived in Estonia for thousands of years, longer than almost any other people has stayed in one European homeland. German crusaders conquered the region in the 1200s, and for the next 700 years Estonians were ruled by Danes, Germans, Swedes, and, from 1710, the Russian Empire. A national awakening in the 1800s revived the language and started the song festivals in 1869. Estonia declared independence in 1918 and defended it in a war against Soviet Russia. In 1940 the Soviet Union seized the country, followed by Nazi occupation and then Soviet rule again, with mass deportations to Siberia. In 1989 two million people joined hands across the Baltic states in a peaceful protest called the Baltic Way, and Estonia regained independence in 1991. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004.
funFacts: Estonia was the first country in the world to allow voting over the internet in a national election, in 2005.
The Kaali crater on Saaremaa island was blasted out by a meteorite about 3,500 years ago and is now a round green pond.
Estonia has more than 2,000 islands, but people live on only about a dozen of them.
Tallinn's town hall pharmacy has been in business since at least 1422, making it one of the oldest in Europe.
Estonians have some of the world's largest per-person collections of folk songs, with more than 130,000 recorded.
